item.description:
作者：Nikunj Kothari 账号：@nikunj 简介：partner @fpvventures - investing in seed/A. previous: early hire @meter, @opendoor, @atlassian & others. love @shimoleejhaveri + 👦👧
ok here’s how we get investors to fomo our series A and get seven term sheets..
first, we have to vague post revenue. or customers. this is absolutely critical. no y axis, just keep showing numbers and to the right. graphs work and of course get your investors to quote tweet it and take credit. they love doing that anyway. make it vague like “slowly but surely” or “i see an exponential when I see one”
ok, once you do that, you know you can do another launch video for features or even better multiple for features so you get maximum airtime. after that case studies are critical - get a trendsetter company to talk about you or even better have the labs mention you in articles. this will guarantee cold emails to grab coffee from partners.
also you know you can buy “articles” in “premier” publications. you can even run ads against it targeted to just investors too. you’re joking? no dead serious bro.
ok now that you have interest and top of mindshare - the most important thing is to use the magic mantras of “large ambition” and combinations of “long horizon agent swarms abilterared world models physical ai”.
and finally and most importantly you don’t have a deck because of course we’re not raising, we were thinking early next year. and of course we still got pre empted so we don’t have a data room even. you get on or not it’s your call.
and then you use the magic words of optimizing for the best partner but let’s be honest we both know i just want the best valuation.
(again the whole thing is satire, but individually each line is true)

With the right harness, a deep understanding of your domain of what you want to build, likely a ...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
This sounds extreme and I wouldn’t have believed it even a year ago, but we’re starting to see plenty of examples of productivity gains that are an order of magnitude or two above output levels pre-AI.
With the right harness, a deep understanding of your domain of what you want to build, likely a relatively new codebase (with some exceptions), a fluency of how to work with multiple agents at once, and a setup that makes it so you can test and deploy with limited friction, outputs on this level feel realistic in coding.
What’s crazy is this gap doesn’t appear to be diminishing over time. You’d think that we’d see a convergence in the lines because of AI, but it turns out the more depth you had before -and willingness now to take a different approach- gives you crazy leverage. And that is only compounding as the models can take on larger work and harder problems.
Right now this is most pronounced in software engineering for the obvious reasons. But there’s no reason we don’t start to see this in a number of other computer-use-sensitive domains like other scientific fields, AEC, finance, cyber, and more. Going to get quite wild.

item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user.
Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after.
And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user.
Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly.
Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.

item.title: Tokenization, Agentic Trading, Harmonic: Robinhood's Mission to Expand Ownership with CEO Vlad Tenev
item.description:
播客：No Priors
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:07 Prediction markets are an evolution of news. You just can see what's happening and what's likely to happen in the future through the odds.
Speaker 2 | 00:07 - 00:11 What is your reaction to the revolution in math that's happening with AI today?
Speaker 1 | 00:11 - 00:20 It's too centralized, right? It's like AI companies with their big data centers and their employees using secret models to sort of do all this work.
Speaker 2 | 00:20 - 00:22 Do you think people will let agents trade for them?
Speaker 1 | 00:22 - 00:32 So AgenTik trading, clearly product market fit. We're seeing really strong adoption. Like, over a 150,000 customers have opened agentic trading accounts with us.
Speaker 2 | 00:32 - 00:53 Many of these things that you describe, institutional traders have the ability to do this, but it's expensive and sophisticated. If that's democratized, what does that mean? Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, I'm here with Vlad Tenev, the founder and CEO of Robinhood.
Speaker 2 | 00:53 - 01:18 We talk about what Robinhood is today as a financial conglomerate trying to expand ownership in the economy from tokenization to prediction markets to how AI agents will trade for everyone in retail. We also talk about Harmonic, his effort to make a math superintelligence, and whether there can be distributed discovery and science rather than centralized. Welcome, Vlad. Vlad, thank you so much for doing this.
Speaker 1 | 01:19 - 01:20 Thank you for having me.
Speaker 2 | 01:20 - 01:28 So everyone knows Robinhood, but it's also evolved a ton as a company. Can you just put it in context for our listeners? Like, what do you... Describe it today.
Speaker 1 | 01:28 - 01:54 We do a lot of things. We're live in some form or another in over 120 countries. And if I had to sum up Robinhood in one word or one idea, it would be ownership. I think we're the ownership company, the companies that's most associated with that. And when I say that, so why does ownership matter?
Speaker 1 | 01:55 - 02:36 I think on an individual basis, people want to own things. It's the tried and true route to financial freedom, financial independence. You know, if you're an asset owner and you accumulate assets over time, it's just the best way to build your wealth. So there's an individual element to it that really, whether you're trading, whether you're accumulating assets, whether you're investing in venture, I think it's very very important. And also, you know, the things you own say a lot about your personality.
Speaker 1 | 02:36 - 03:20 It's almost like, it becomes like a part of your identity. Like, if it's a car collection or your collectibles, your cards, your stock portfolio. I think there's a lot of individuality into it. So I think there's an individual benefit, but I think there's also a collective benefit, the sense that a society without broad ownership is inherently very unstable. It's a fragile society, and if you have more people that own things, they're more bought in, they have more stake in the outcome, and they become kind of defenders and protectors of the system.
Speaker 1 | 03:20 - 04:15 So I think especially now when people are kind of pushing back against society and it feels a little bit fraught with AI and all of this disruption, I think giving people the ability to own companies at earlier stages is increasingly important. So it's really what ties together all of our things from Trump accounts, which is ownership at age zero, Robinhood Ventures, ownership of private companies before they go public. Tokenization, you can think of as ownership gone global. Like how can we make all the people outside The US, people in 120 plus countries that don't sometimes even have functional banking systems, how can we kind of plug them into this economic fabric of society? So yeah, that's how I think about it.
Speaker 1 | 04:15 - 04:37 We started off as just a simple app to buy stocks at zero commissions on your phone, and then we've kind of expanded from that into an increasingly global financial conglomerate that allows customers to own things across a wide variety of surfaces and asset classes.
Speaker 2 | 04:37 - 05:06 You might be the only large financial I think of as a missionary organization, with the other being like Vanguard or something like that. Can we talk about how you got here? Like, you know, so you... I learned recently that you studied math under Terence Tau, and you worked on HFT. Neither of those sound like a missionary for people, if may say that.
Speaker 2 | 05:06 - 05:11 How did you discover this mission or, you know, come to it? Yeah.
Speaker 1 | 05:11 - 06:04 Yeah, so, I mean, rewinding back even further, I was born in Eastern Europe in the late 80s, kind of on the brink of the collapse of the Soviet Union and the lifting of the Iron Curtain, and actually in the nineteen ninety's, so I immigrated to The US after my parents. My dad had an opportunity to come study at the University of Delaware for his master's, and then was also was able to take advantage of that and stay in America full time. And so my mom came about a year after, and I came about six months after her, which was a pretty unique experience. I mean, talk to a lot of parents. I didn't see my dad for a year and a half and my mom for six months when I was a small child.
Speaker 1 | 06:04 - 06:38 I lived with my grandparents and a large portion of that was we just didn't have the money to send the whole family. So we had to, you know, we weren't sure that my dad would have a long term future in this country. So we thought maybe he'd come back after a year or two years. And anyway, he did quite well and was able to send for my mom and then me. And my last year in Bulgaria, 1991, the inflation rate was something like 170% in Bulgaria.
Speaker 1 | 06:38 - 07:15 So my early memories were the rolling blackouts, and you know, my family huddled around the radio, which was battery operated, just listening to what was going on. The lines at the bodega which I could see from my window for buying milk and eggs, the milk would come in these big plastic bags, and you know, the one week a year you would get bananas from other communist countries. So Cuba would, the Cuban bananas I remember were just amazing. And then I would come to The US and there were just bananas everywhere, right? But they weren't as good.
Speaker 1 | 07:17 - 07:56 And so, yeah, and even after I moved, in 1997 Bulgaria had the unfortunate distinction of having the number one inflation rate in the world. It was something like 2000% annualized, so they were just adding zeros to the currency every couple of months. And so from that point I just developed kind of an understanding of money. I had to be very independent. Parents, it was always a topic of conversation, and we'd have to send money to my grandparents back home as they were dealing with this inflation crisis, and my grandparents actually would keep their assets in copper cookware.
Speaker 1 | 07:56 - 08:23 So there was this closet in my grandfather's house where, you know, he worked as a doctor kind of in the shipbuilding and naval industries, so he was on a boat a lot of times. So he had his contacts at the port, and as soon as he would get salary, he would exchange it for copper cookware. So it was kind of the first real world asset that I encountered people Like, investing
Speaker 2 | 08:24 - 08:25 sorry, stacked like pans.
Speaker 1 | 08:25 - 08:28 Exactly. Yeah, In the closet you'd have.
Speaker 2 | 08:28 - 08:29 Holds value,
Speaker 1 | 08:29 - 09:06 Pots and pans, much better than the local currency at the time. And so, I just, I grew up with that. I grew up understanding, you know, what happens in a broken system where you don't have free markets and good healthy capital markets. And I'd say for me, I pretty quickly discovered that academically I was quite strong, and also independent. Basically by choice, yo...
